statement: For 2023 KTM changed nearly everything: new hydroformed chromoly frame with a forged shock mount and reworked stiffness, engine rotated 2 degrees back so the countershaft sprocket sits 3 mm lower, higher compression, new airbox, hollow die-cast swingarm, shorter and lighter WP XACT shock (15 mm shorter, about 100 g lighter), fork Hydrostops, quickshifter, and bigger die-cast footpegs moved inward.
notes: Shock length/weight from a magazine 2023 race test; footpeg size from Enduro21; rest from a magazine First Look (KTM press data).

source.name: Motocross Action: First Look 2023 KTM 450SXF/350SXF/250SXF

statement: 2024 was a carry-over year: new graphics with purple accents, fork and shock valving taken from the 2023.5 Factory Edition, shock high-speed compression shim stack grown from 15 to 23 shims for finer adjustment, a better-sealed start/stop switch, and a one-piece air inlet sleeve/snorkel. MSRP $11,099.
notes: A magazine race test (magazine reporting of KTM changes); one-piece snorkel listed in a magazine 2024 FE guide.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2024 KTM 450SXF

statement: The 2025 450 SX-F got the Factory Edition frame (cut-outs and thinner walls at the head tube, engine mounts and shock tower, about 300 g lighter), shorter and slimmer shock linkage arms with smaller bolts and new seals, reworked fork settings, revised shock geometry for more linkage ground clearance, a swingarm with a lowered top and thicker/machined chain slider, a new silencer, new bi-composite tank shrouds, a one-piece stiffer air inlet sleeve, a stronger rear brake pedal, a new chain guide, and Dunlop Geomax MX34 tyres.
notes: Combined from KTM model page, a magazine/Bikesales range reports and a magazine tech page (MSRP).

source.name: KTM 2025 450 SX-F model page

statement: Testers report that 2025 engine changes were mostly ECU, quickshifter, throttle-body and reliability tweaks plus a new silencer that KTM says sharpens response with the map switch and is slightly quieter; the quickshifter gained two reaction speeds.
notes: A magazine describes the changes without part-level detail; KTM page confirms silencer claim.

source.name: Motocross Action: MXA Race Test 2025 KTM 450SXF

statement: 2026 changes were minimal: a threaded radiator cap that opens with less force, a protection cap on the CPC fuel connector, new graphics, and (per a magazine) a black powder-coated frame and black seat. MSRP $11,649.
notes: A magazine First Look 2026 lists the frame colour; a magazine lists price and changes.

source.name: Dirt Rider: 2026 KTM 450 SX-F Technical Overview

statement: KTM calls the 2027 450 SX-F largely unchanged: in-mould graphics with red, re-routed wiring harness with new fixing points to reduce wear, unspecified engine updates for rideability and to meet the latest FIM/AMA sound rules, and frame wording about shock-mount, engine-mount and wall-thickness optimisation. US bikes arrive late spring 2026.
notes: The frame text may repeat the 2025 frame description rather than describe a new frame; no 2027 dyno or test data found yet.

source.name: KTM South Africa 2027 450 SX-F page

notes: Same dyno and bike as map-2 run.

statement: A magazine measured 56.3 hp at about 9,500 rpm and 48 Nm (about 35.4 lb-ft) just before 7,000 rpm. The curve is steep with a slight dip between 7,000 and 8,500 rpm and loses up to about 2 hp past peak before the 11,000 rpm ceiling.

notes: Later, some tuners offered stock-ECU remaps (see community records).

topic: aftermarket ECU: AIM Taipan and Vortex
statement: A tester preferred an AIM Taipan ECU: per-gear mapping gave a longer-pulling second gear, smoother low end and stronger mid-to-top with better exit traction. A Vortex unit mapped with a tuner also beat stock. Both let him ride a gear higher with less engine braking.
notes: No dyno numbers published.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Testing: 2023 KTM 450 SX-F suspension baseline / chassis tips

statement: Owners report tuners reprogramming Vortex units for 2023+ KTMs (about $1,100 from a tuner), a tuner remaps of stock ECUs, and that older Vortex units may not support the stock map switch, traction control or quickshift. One tuner reportedly said it cannot work on 2023+ ECUs.
notes: A magazine threads Jan 2025 and Nov 2025-Jan 2026; mostly 350 SX-F owners, same ECU family. Results mixed.

statement: The electronic power valve must be re-taught its end stops after the cylinder is removed: plug in the brand's wake-up dongle with throttle held at half for 10 seconds, then release so the valve cycles. Skipping it can make the bike bog or not rev.
notes: Procedure as described by a magazine from dealer practice; each brand (KTM/Husqvarna/GasGas) uses its own dongle.

statement: The carbureted KTM 250 power valve starts opening at about 5,600 rpm with stock preload and is fully open at about 7,900 rpm with the stock yellow inner spring. Each full turn of the preload screw moves the opening point about 150 rpm.
notes: A magazine figures; a magazine Magazine gives identical numbers. Article covers KTM 250SX/300 (carbureted, pre-2023); mechanical design shared by Husqvarna and GasGas 250s. Likely the same figures are reprinted from KTM's own guidance.

topic: power valve preload screw - direction and feel
statement: Turning the preload screw clockwise (in) gives smoother power and broader bottom end; counterclockwise (out) gives more hit and maximum top end. Adjust in 1/8 turns; total range is six turns.
notes: CONFLICT on direction: a magazine 'This much we know' and a magazine say one turn out opens the valve 150 rpm sooner (smoother) and in opens later (more hit), the opposite of a magazine Ask the MXperts text. See conflicts. Do not loosen the two screws holding the brass adjuster body.

statement: Stock TBI mapping is conservative and runs flat into the rev limiter; a tuner remap kept the easy bottom end, added throttle response and mid-to-top pull, and reduced limiter hits. Pipe-specific maps exist (FMF, a tuner, DR.D).
notes: No dyno numbers published. A tester (2023 300SX) described stock as rich and lethargic and the remap as adding low-rpm response and 2nd/3rd gear pull. Tuners such as WMR and Jamie Ellis cracked the locked ECU.

statement: The YZ250 power valve is driven by a crank-gear centrifugal governor and has three pieces: a center valve that opens in the first half of control-rod rotation and two side valves that open in the second half, held by torsion springs that default it closed.
notes: Description from US patent 9,797,275 (aftermarket inventor describing the stock 1999-on design). The patent attributes the YZ250's mid-rpm 'hit' to the center valve reaching its stop, where friction and spring force cause hesitation then surge.

notes: Description from US patent 9,797,275 (aftermarket inventor describing the stock 1999-on design). The patent attributes the YZ250's mid-rpm 'hit' to the center valve reaching its stop, where friction and spring force cause hesitation then surge.

statement: Yamaha softened the YZ250X by raising head volume from 21.5 to 23.6 cc (compression 8.9 to 7.9:1), raising the exhaust port 0.5 mm with a matching valve shape, retarding the CDI in the mid-to-high range, and setting the governor spring/preload to open the valve sooner; the pipe is 35 mm narrower.
notes: Yamaha changes as reported by a magazine. Result: milder hit, tractable to 6,500 rpm, dip at 7,000 picking up at 7,400, same peak around 8,800 rpm, more over-rev. A real-world example of how head volume, port height, ignition and PV timing move a two-stroke's power.

statement: In a magazine 2020 test the YZ250 made its best power higher in the rpm and did not like being lugged, needing clutch out of corners, while the KTM/Husky 250s were better low-to-mid; the YZ was slower but easier to ride.
notes: Conflicts with a magazine 2015/2016 shootout which called the YZ250 broad with enough low-end torque; see conflicts.

source.name: Motocross Action - Race test 2020 Yamaha YZ250

statement: A a tuner Works pipe and 304 silencer took the 2022 YZ125 from 34.4 hp at 11,500 to 35.8 hp at 11,600 rpm; no change below 9,500 rpm, then faster build, broader top and more over-rev.
notes: Jetting used: main 162, pilot 72, clip up, air screw 3.5 out. Pre-2022 YZ125 pipes do not fit the 2022 engine.

statement: A magazine says aftermarket pipes add about 2 hp to the YZ125; porting works best combined with raised compression, which means milling the cylinder base (lowering all ports) and re-chambering the head, and usually race gas. A tuner standard pipe favors top end, its RV pipe low-mid.
notes: Reeds: Boyesen Rad Valve for mid-to-top, Moto Tassinari VForce4 to broaden the midrange. GYTR flywheel weights fill the powerband and extend top end.

source.name: Motocross Action - Race test 2021 Yamaha YZ125

statement: Robbie Wageman's 2026 race YZ is bored from 66.4 to 72 mm (293.2 cc) on the stock 72 mm stroke with a modified three-piece power valve, reworked head and ports, V-Force 4 reeds and FMF exhaust.
notes: A tuner dyno-tuned jetting and ignition; numbers not published.

source.name: Dirt Bike - Robbie Wageman team 2026 YZ250-based YZ300 race bike

statement: Owners re-time the YZ250 governor by swapping two 1.0 mm thrust washers for 0.8 mm YZ250X washers and removing one, cutting spring preload by about 1.4 mm so the valve opens earlier; it fills the off-idle dip but needs a leaner power jet (#35 reported).
notes: Spring data quoted in thread: stock YZ spring 0.640 in installed, ~18 lb preload, 40 lb at full compression; YZ250X spring 0.672 in, 19-20 lb preload, 52-53 lb.

statement: On the VHM 250 TBI head, going from the 22.6 cc to the 21.4 cc insert raises full-stroke compression by roughly 0.6 of a ratio point, which is why the smaller insert calls for 105 RON fuel.
notes: CR = (249 + Vc)/Vc: (249+21.4)/21.4 = 12.64; (249+22.6)/22.6 = 12.02. Assumes VHM insert volume is the whole clearance volume, which it may not be (squish gap and gasket not included), so absolute ratios are indicative only. Trapped (exhaust-closed) compression is much lower and needs port height, which is unpublished.

statement: The 250s are undersquare (66.4/72 = 0.92), the 300 is square (1.00) and the 125s are near square (0.99). At their measured peaks, all run about 20.4-20.9 m/s mean piston speed: 250SX 20.6 m/s at 8,600, YZ250 20.9 at 8,700, 300SX 20.4 at 8,500, KTM 125 20.3 at 11,200, YZ125 20.5 at 11,300 rpm.
notes: Mean piston speed = 2 x stroke(mm) x rpm / 60000. Peak rpm from a magazine dynos (2024 250SX, 2013 YZ250, 2023 300SX, 2021 KTM 125SX, 2022 YZ125). Similar piston speeds at peak suggest both brands tune ports/pipes to similar gas-flow limits; the 125s peak higher purely because of their shorter stroke.

At their measured peaks, all run about 20.4-20.9 m/s mean piston speed: 250SX 20.6 m/s at 8,600, YZ250 20.9 at 8,700, 300SX 20.4 at 8,500, KTM 125 20.3 at 11,200, YZ125 20.5 at 11,300 rpm.
notes: Mean piston speed = 2 x stroke(mm) x rpm / 60000. Peak rpm from a magazine dynos (2024 250SX, 2013 YZ250, 2023 300SX, 2021 KTM 125SX, 2022 YZ125). Similar piston speeds at peak suggest both brands tune ports/pipes to similar gas-flow limits; the 125s peak higher purely because of their shorter stroke.

statement: More flywheel inertia smooths delivery and helps traction but slows how fast the engine revs; Yamaha added 21% flywheel inertia to the 2022 YZ125 to match its higher output, and tuners use GYTR flywheel weights to fill the powerband.
notes: A magazine credits the YZ125's quick-revving midrange feel to low flywheel effect.

source.name: Motocross Action - Race test 2021 Yamaha YZ125

topic: principle - ignition timing and power valve on feel (Yamaha example)
statement: Yamaha's own softening recipe for the YZ250X combines mid-to-high rpm ignition retard, earlier power-valve opening and lower compression; the result is a milder hit and broader pull with the same peak, showing how these three levers interact.
notes: Interpretation of Yamaha's documented changes; see 2t record on YZ250 vs YZ250X.

source.name: Motocross Action - Ask the MXperts: the X factor versus the non-X factor

topic: Power Tuner app: what it is and how it talks to the bike
statement: The Power Tuner app is free for iOS and Android and connects wirelessly (Wi-Fi from the bike's Communication Control Unit, CCU) to the bike's CAN-bus. It adjusts air/fuel mixture and ignition timing, sets traction and launch control, runs a lap timer, keeps a race log and shows diagnostics, maintenance and engine run time.

vals.link: Wi-Fi to on-bike CCU, CAN-bus network

notes: Yamaha US 2025 YZ450F page. CCU named on Yamaha's Power Tuner page (placement of CCU affects signal). WR models in the US need a GYTR CCU accessory (see GYTR records).

source.name: Yamaha Motor USA, 2025 YZ450F features page

statement: To connect, the bike's CCU must be powered (owners report pressing the start button), then join the bike's Wi-Fi network on the phone using the password printed on the CCU label, and accept the 'no internet' warning. The label is reached by removing the left side panel/number plate and pulling out the Wi-Fi box.

vals.password_location: label on CCU (Wi-Fi box) behind left side panel / left number plate

notes: Owner reports 2018-2024. A magazine 2023 YZ250F race test independently describes the password under the serial number on the Wi-Fi box behind the left side panel. Fixes reported: allow app local-network permission, allow networks without internet, try another phone, on iPhone set a manual IP; a missing CCU means no network.

statement: A magazine procedure: connect to the bike's Wi-Fi, open Map List in the app, add a new map, type in the fuel and ignition grids, then send it to the bike with the up-arrow button. A magazine found the process harder than it should be.
notes: Magazine procedure description, 2023 YZ250F.

topic: Power Tuner fuel/ignition grid size (app listing)
statement: Yamaha's app listing says fuel injection and ignition can be fine-tuned on a 4x4 grid (16 cells each) of engine speed versus throttle opening, as two separate grids (FI and IG).
notes: Listing text applies to the current app (2026). Grid breakpoints for 2023+ bikes are not stated by Yamaha; see the throttle-axis and breakpoint records.

statement: A tester map that adds low-end excitement to fill the gap before the strong mid-range hit, smoothing the bottom-to-mid transition and helping second-gear mid-range roll-on without the bike running away 50-100 ft out of a corner.
notes: Map values in image only.

statement: A magazine answer to the 450's barky low end is a map that adds fuel between 2,000 and 5,000 rpm to take away crispness off idle; Yamaha's optional Smooth Linear map did not tame the low end enough for a magazine. A magazine pairs it with a 48-tooth rear sprocket (stock 49).
notes: Same richer-low-rpm approach in a magazine March 2023 race test. A magazine says it tested three maps on the 2025 YZ450F and was not satisfied with any yet (Aug 2024). Chart image URL could not be fetched.

statement: A Yamaha R&D map that adds pulling power when shifting through second, third and fourth gears.
notes: Stated for 2022-2023 YZ250F (same engine).

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested, 2023 Yamaha YZ250F Optional Yamaha Power Tuner Maps

statement: A tester map with less engine braking and a more balanced chassis feel off the throttle; owners of 2024 bikes report it adds bottom and top and is very similar to a tester map.
notes: 2024 owner comments from a magazine forum (COMMUNITY).

topic: 'a tester' map by Yamaha test rider (2024 YZ250F)
statement: Yamaha test rider Steve Tokarski's map cleans up the rich feel at low rpm and adds excitement from the crack of the throttle into the low-mid; it was run with traction control off.
notes: Owners say it is very similar to a tester Free Feeling with slightly more engine braking (a magazine forum, Nov 2023).

source.name: PulpMX, Ten things about the 2024 Yamaha YZ250F on track

statement: Owners report the 2024 YZ250F stock map has less bottom and more mid/top than 2022; the 'Responsive' map gets the low end back but hits harder; 'a tester' and 'a tester Free Feeling' add bottom and top.
notes: Small number of owners; no values.

source.name: Vital MX forum, 2024 YZ 250F Review thread

topic: A tester 2026 YZ450F map (less engine braking)
statement: The tester found the 2026 YZ450F has more engine braking than 2024-2025, making it hard to roll corners and upsetting the chassis; his map relaxes the engine on deceleration to fix corner-entry balance.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested, 2026 Yamaha YZ450F Optional Yamaha Power Tuner Map

topic: A tuner / Jamie Ellis map (2024 YZ450F)
statement: A magazine test bike ran a map from Jamie Ellis of a tuner to make the 450 manageable for average riders, noting the throttle-opening (TH%) settings on the vertical axis make a big difference.
notes: A magazine says the 450 needs detuning, not hot-rodding, for most riders; biggest power gain 7,500-10,000 rpm.

source.name: Dirt Bike, Riding the 2024 Yamaha YZ450F long term: the wrap

topic: YZ450FX tester maps (Magic Map, JL Smooth)
statement: On the 2023 YZ450FX, Yamaha's 'Magic Map' softened the initial hit while keeping pull (some said it revved like a 350) and suited motocross and fast terrain but was abrupt in tight, low-traction ground; the tester-made 'JL Smooth' map was preferred for tight terrain and let riders lug it with little clutch.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2023 Yamaha YZ450FX test

topic: YZ450FX maps and traction control in mud
statement: On the 2024 YZ450FX the tester ran the mellow map 2 most of the day in muddy, tight terrain, softened both maps further and added traction control through the app.
notes: TC level not stated.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2024 Yamaha YZ450FX off-road racer first impression

statement: Testers preferred the standard map on the 2025 YZ250F; the performance map adds mid and top but takes away too much bottom in places.

source.name: Dirt Bike Test, 2025 Yamaha YZ250F first impression

statement: An owner set every cell to -10 fuel and -10 ignition on a 2023 YZ450F; the rpm built more slowly and power dropped, making the bike feel like a 350 on one map and a full 450 on the other.
notes: Single owner video. Note: in this app minus fuel is leaner, which normally sharpens response; the owner's result is reported as-is.

source.name: YouTube, mxengineer1: 2023 YZ450F turned into YZ350F with Yamaha Power Tuner

topic: What fuel and ignition changes do to the feel (Yamaha test rider guidance)
statement: More fuel gives a smoother response and slower rpm rise; less fuel gives quicker response and faster rpm rise. More ignition advance sharpens response and adds a little perceived power; retard softens it. More fuel plus more advance gives slower revving with a stronger torque feel.
notes: Change one region at a time and switch back to the other map to confirm the feel.

topic: Dyno effect of Power Tuner maps (2024 YZ450F)
statement: On a Dyno Dynamics dyno the stock 2024 YZ450F made 56.4 hp at 9,500 rpm; about two hours of leaner fuel and more advance gained only 0.6 hp with more torque across most of the range (too much advance made it too aggressive to ride), while maximum fuel and maximum retard cut peak to 51.4 hp with a much gentler, slower-revving feel that still revved past 11,000 rpm.
notes: Dyno Tech (Melbourne), Dyno Dynamics dyno; stock exhaust and air filter; fuel not stated. Article notes US Dynojets usually read higher. Tuned peak is DERIVED (56.4 + 0.6).

source.name: Australasian Dirt Bike, 2024 Yamaha YZ450F dyno test

vals.unlocks: full throttle; 2 pre-programmed maps selectable in app

topic: Yamaha's WR mapping ideas (soft / medium / aggressive)
statement: Yamaha Australia's WR guide: a Soft map adds fuel at low rpm and retards ignition (with higher traction control) for beginners and slippery or technical trails; Medium adjusts fuel through the midrange for drive; Aggressive leans slightly and advances ignition with TC off for open terrain and experienced riders. Testers liked Medium best on the WR450F.

vals.soft: +fuel low rpm, ignition retarded, TC higher
vals.medium: midrange fuel tuned, ignition softened in key areas
vals.aggressive: slightly leaner, advanced ignition, TC off

notes: Qualitative only. Applies to WR but the fuel/ignition logic carries over to YZ.

statement: For 2025 Yamaha revised the rear linkage and shock settings, updated fork settings (delta-shaped piston shims), changed the front engine mounts, increased clutch-plate oil holes from 6 to 18, added a raised-rib handlebar switchbox, and fitted lighter aluminum footpeg brackets.

statement: Testers report the 2025 front engine mounts went back to a single piece after two years of two thinner pieces, the throttle tube was moved out 10 mm to reduce blisters, and the MSRP stayed $9,999.
notes: A magazine describes the 2025 linkage as stiffer and the spring rate softer, with new ECU map settings (mxa25v). Yamaha's 2025 US spec page later showed $10,299 MSRP; a magazine reported $9,999 at launch.

statement: 2026 brought a redesigned intake port (stronger tumble, more linear low-mid response), new intake and exhaust resonators for noise rules, a new frame with a thinner front downtube, a new KYB shock with hand-adjustable low-speed compression, revised fork settings, a standard hydraulic clutch with new inner hub, and a password ECU lock in the Power Tuner app.
notes: A magazine lists the hydraulic clutch under the YZ250F section, but the Yamaha USA release text (GateDrop) and Yamaha Australia (MCNews) confirm it for the YZ450F.

source.name: GateDrop, 2026 YZ450F revealed (Yamaha USA release)

statement: A magazine reports the 2026 engine also got a new cam, flywheel inertia up 8%, a head-pipe resonator and new muffler; clutch spring tension up 10%; and stock rear sprocket changed from 49 to 51 teeth. Frame: more lateral rigidity at the forged downtube, softer engine cradle, changed engine hangers, top shock mount less vertically rigid; geometry unchanged.
notes: Magazine-reported technical briefing details; not found in Yamaha USA public spec pages.

statement: Australian launch info lists 2026 shock main-valve ports up from 4 to 6, base valve piston enlarged from 24 mm to 28 mm with two-way oil passages, a piston cooler, a new magneto, front engine mount thickness 6 mm and asymmetric rear engine mounts.
